title: Teachers Need More Than the Curriculum
author: Jo Lein
summary: Jo Lein argues that even the strongest curriculum cannot substitute for the teacher's own knowledge of what to do when students struggle — specifically, the diagnostic and instructional knowledge needed to bridge students into difficult reading. The article is structured around a 'know/do' chart for effective literacy instruction, designed for contexts with many multilingual learners, that maps the teacher knowledge and concrete actions needed at each stage of a reading lesson. Lein's central complaint is that instructional language ('scaffold the text,' 'differentiate,' 'check for understanding') often functions as professional jargon without operational content: teachers know the words but cannot translate them into specific, learnable actions. The piece argues that curriculum gives teachers what students should read, but leaves critical gaps around how to build background knowledge, which vocabulary actually needs to be taught, where to stop and model, how to diagnose the difference between a decoding problem and a comprehension problem, and how to structure talk so students produce language rather than silence. The article is part 2 of a series and points forward to structural school design as the next layer of the problem.
points: Curriculum tells teachers what students should read and do; it does not reliably tell them how to bridge students who lack the background knowledge, vocabulary, and language skills to engage with that material.

The 'know/do' chart is a practical tool for making teacher knowledge explicit: naming what a teacher needs to know (background knowledge building, vocabulary selection, decoding diagnosis) alongside what a teacher needs to be able to do at each instructional stage.

Big instructional words ('scaffold,' 'differentiate,' 'CFU') carry meaning for experienced practitioners but produce professional scar tissue for others — they need to be operationalized into specific, observable actions before they can be learned.

The diagnostic question — 'Is this a decoding problem, a fluency problem, a vocabulary problem, or a language problem?' — is identified as one of the most important knowledge teachers need, because the intervention for each is different.

The 'survive Thursday afternoon' standard for good practice is the article's most memorable formulation: a strategy that works on Monday during professional development but cannot survive the reality of a hard Thursday is not actually a strategy teachers can use.
quotes: Knowing where to click is not the same as knowing what to do next. Alignment This is the alignment I want us to get better at: Student need → teacher knowledge → instructional action.
We find a strategy we like and go looking for a student problem to attach it to. Teacher knowledge and skills We use a lot of big instructional words…scaffold, differentiate, CFU.

They can also mean absolutely nothing to a new teacher and trigger a whole lot of professional scar tissue for an experienced one. “Check for understanding.” What evidence am I collecting, and what am I supposed to do with it?
If we want good practice to be visible, learnable, and repeatable, we have to name what teachers need to know and be able to do. I think many teachers know what students are supposed to complete.

I am less convinced we have consistently taught them how to bridge students into difficult reading. How do I know whether a student has a decoding problem, a fluency problem, a vocabulary problem, or a language problem?

How do I structure talk so students actually produce language? In true backward-planning fashion, I decided to create a know/do chart for our vision of effective literacy instruction, specifically for my students, who are primarily multilingual learners.

[ ] Good practice has to survive Thursday afternoon This must be our new standard: Can the practice survive Thursday afternoon? You know…the hard text, three students absent, and a Chromebook update appearing at the worst possible moment.
